concepts.name: The four parts of a STAR answer
Action: your own steps and reasons, in the first person
Result: a number, and what you learned
A small bank of stories that covers the common questions

questions.prompt: In a STAR answer, which part answers "What was your goal, and what were you responsible for?"

choices.text: Situation
Task
Action
Result

questions.explanation: Amazon's guide defines Task as your goal and what you were responsible for, which tells the interviewer your role. Situation sets the scene, Action is what you did, and Result is how it turned out. Mixing Situation and Task is common; keep them short and separate.

questions.prompt: A practice answer spends 90 of its 120 seconds on project background. Which advice does it break?

choices.text: Give just enough background for the big picture, then move on to your actions
Always open with the Result, then go back and explain the Situation in full
Never mention the project's context, since interviewers only score your actions
Keep every STAR part to exactly the same length, about thirty seconds each

questions.explanation: Amazon asks for just enough background to understand the big picture and what made it challenging. Most of the time should go on your actions and the result. Its tips also say to balance detail with clarity, then pause and ask whether the interviewer wants more context.

questions.prompt: Read aloud, one of your stories runs three and a half minutes. Explain what you would cut and what you would keep to get it under two minutes.

model_answer.summary: Cut background and team detail down to what the listener needs, and keep your own actions, your reasons, and a result with a number. Offer more context at the end instead of saying it all up front.
key_points: Shrink the Situation to just enough background for the big picture
Keep your own actions and why you took them; cut what other people did
Keep a Result with a number and one thing you learned
End by pausing and offering more detail if the interviewer wants it

questions.explanation: Amazon's tips ask for answers that are clear and concise but complete, and suggest pausing to ask whether the interviewer wants more context. The interviewer is assessing your behaviour, so time spent on others' work or long background is the first thing to cut.

questions.prompt: Which Action sentence best follows Amazon's advice?

choices.text: "We improved the retrieval pipeline a lot, and the whole team was really happy with it."
"After some discussion, the team decided to add a reranker and lower the top-k to 5."
"I always write tests first and check the traces carefully, on every project I work on."
"I added a reranker and cut top-k from 20 to 5, as traces showed irrelevant chunks."

questions.explanation: Amazon asks you to focus on your individual contribution, use "I" instead of "we", and give real examples rather than generalisations. The last option says what you did and why. "We" and "the team" hide your part, and "I always..." is a generalisation, not one situation.

questions.prompt: Explain why the Action part of a STAR story should use "I", and why it should include your reasons and the alternatives you considered.

model_answer.summary: The interviewer is judging your behaviour, so they need to hear what you did yourself. Your reasons and rejected alternatives show how you make decisions, not just what happened.
key_points: Amazon asks you to focus on your individual contributions and to say "I" rather than "we", even for team work
The Tech Interview Handbook describes Action as what you did, why you did it and what the alternatives were
Reasons and alternatives show your judgement (the "why" of your decisions)
A "we" story leaves the interviewer unable to tell what you contributed

questions.explanation: Behavioural interviews look for evidence that you have shown the right behaviours before. A clear first-person account with reasons gives the interviewer that evidence. Using "I" doesn't mean taking credit for others' work: name the team, then describe your part.

questions.prompt: Which Result is strongest for a "cost or latency win" story?

choices.text: "p95 latency fell from 4.1 s to 1.3 s and cost per request fell 38%; I learned to profile first."
"It went really well, it was much faster, and everyone was pleased with the outcome of the project."
"The client was happy with the speed and said they would recommend us to other people."
"We shipped it in the end, a bit later than planned, but it worked fine and felt quicker."

questions.explanation: Amazon asks you to say what happened because of your actions, back it with numbers if you have them, and share what you learned. The first option has a before-and-after number and a lesson. The others are claims the interviewer can't weigh.

questions.prompt: The Tech Interview Handbook mentions a STAR variant called STARR. What does the extra R add?

choices.text: A recommendation for the company
The risks you took
Reflection: what you learned and how you grew
A reference the interviewer can contact

questions.explanation: The handbook describes STAR(R), or STARR, as STAR plus a reflection on what you learned and how you grew. Amazon's own Result guidance asks for the same thing: what you accomplished and what you learned.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks, "Tell me about a time a project failed." Explain how you would structure the answer so it helps you rather than hurts you.

model_answer.summary: Tell a real failure in STAR form, own your part in the first person, state the outcome honestly, and end with what you learned and what you now do differently.
key_points: Choose a real failure; Amazon says not every story has to be a success
Describe your own actions with "I" and take ownership rather than blaming others
State the result honestly, with numbers where you have them
End with what you learned and what you changed afterwards

questions.explanation: Amazon lists taking a risk, making a mistake or failing as a typical question, and says what matters is what you learned and how you grew. It also values honesty and self-awareness over a perfect record. An answer that dodges into a disguised success usually lands worse than an honest one.

questions.prompt: Why prepare a small set of rich stories rather than a script for every possible question?

choices.text: Interviewers ask exactly six behavioural questions, so six stories cover them all
A few stories showing repeatable behaviours can be adapted to many questions
Interviewers prefer scripted answers, because they sound more polished and confident
Amazon requires exactly one prepared story for each of its Leadership Principles

questions.explanation: The handbook advises 3–5 key stories from high-impact projects where you were directly involved, told to show behaviours that repeat, rather than memorising answers to every question. Amazon says it doesn't expect rehearsed scripts. One strong story can answer a conflict question and an ownership question from different angles.

questions.prompt: Which three questions does the Tech Interview Handbook say to prepare for first?

choices.text: Strengths, weaknesses and salary expectations
Why this company, why this role, and where you see yourself in five years
Your biggest failure, your biggest success and your hardest bug
Tell me about yourself, your most impactful project, and a time you resolved a conflict

questions.explanation: The handbook calls these three the most common behavioural questions and says to prepare them first. Your six stories should at least cover them: the project pitch and the conflict story are both in this week's set.
